title: Online Safety Bill 2021
portfolio: Communications, Urban Infrastructure, Cities and the Arts

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would create a new regulatory system for online safety in Australia.
It would replace the current online content scheme, expand the cyber-bullying scheme beyond social media, and give the eSafety Commissioner new powers.
The eSafety Commissioner could require internet service providers to block access to some violent material for limited periods during crises.
changes: retain and replicate existing provisions from the Enhancing Online Safety Act 2015.
create a removal notice scheme for cyber-abuse against adults.
reduce the response time for service providers to removal notices from 48 to 24 hours.
summary.affected: Australians using the internet, including children and adults affected by cyber-bullying, cyber-abuse, and non-consensual sharing of intimate images, as well as service providers like social media, app distribution, and internet search companies, and internet service providers.

speeches.speaker: Paul Fletcher
speeches.brief: The bill, together with the Online Safety Bill 2021, repeals the Enhancing Online Safety Act 2015 and transitions online content regulation to a new Online Safety Act. It increases the maximum penalty for using a carriage service to menace, harass or cause offence from three to five years’ imprisonment, and adjusts penalties for repeated dissemination of private sexual material.

speeches.speaker: Tim Watts
speeches.brief: The Labor speaker supported the Online Safety Bill's objectives but criticised the government’s two-and-a-half-year delay and mismanaged consultation, noting that only 7 technical amendments resulted from 376 submissions and citing unresolved concerns over the adult cyberabuse scheme's clarity, freedom of speech, and the omission of hate speech targeting groups. They moved an amendment recording these failures.

speeches.speaker: Anne Aly
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Online Safety Bill 2021's intent but raised concerns about rushed consultation (only 376 submissions), inadequate checks and balances on the eSafety Commissioner, and the adult cyberabuse scheme potentially being used to silence those calling out racism rather than removing racist content.

speeches.speaker: Brian Mitchell
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the Online Safety Bill 2021 is a necessary but "half cooked" piece of legislation, criticising the government for rushing it after two years of inaction since the 2018 Briggs review, and raised concerns about the eSafety Commissioner's unchecked powers, potential mission creep, and risks to free speech and journalism.

speeches.speaker: Julian Simmonds
speeches.brief: The speaker argued in support of the Online Safety Bill 2021, citing statistics that 80% of four-year-olds use the internet, 30% have their own device, and only 52% of parents discuss online safety, and called for technology companies to be held accountable as publishers with the same rules online as in the real world.

speeches.speaker: George Christensen
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Online Safety Bill will empower the eSafety Commissioner to remove harmful online content, citing statistics that 69% of boys and 23% of girls view X-rated material by age 13, 88% of explicit content contains violence against women, and 42% of teenagers are bullied on Instagram; they also called on the minister to mandate that companies like Google, Apple and Microsoft provide the same parental control features they offer to businesses.

speeches.speaker: Nicolle Flint
speeches.brief: The Online Safety Bill 2021 is essential to protect Australians from online bullying, harassment, and sexist abuse, and the speaker cited her own experience of being stalked and harassed online by a man charged by South Australia Police, as well as the abusive tweets of former journalist Mike Carlton targeting herself and other conservative women like Rita Panahi, Daisy Cousens, Judith Sloan, and Sharri Markson.

speeches.speaker: Tim Wilson
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Online Safety Bill 2021 is necessary to ensure conduct unacceptable offline is not allowed online, particularly to protect children from cyberbullying, revenge porn, and harassment, and to hold platforms accountable. He cited the Christchurch terrorist attacks as a reason for stopping abhorrent violent content online.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Gee
speeches.brief: The speaker thanked contributors and acknowledged the member for Boothby’s courage in sharing her experiences. The Online Safety Bill 2021 requires industry to prevent online harms and introduces new protections for Australians.

speeches.speaker: Paul Fletcher
speeches.brief: The government has committed over $100 million to the eSafety Commissioner and introduced the Online Safety Bill to expand her powers, including a new scheme targeting serious cyberabuse against adults, prioritising safety over big tech profits.

speeches.speaker: Anne Webster
speeches.brief: The committee's third scrutiny report of 2021 examined 11 new bills and 52 legislative instruments, seeking further information on the Online Safety Bill 2021 and suggesting amendments to the Migration and Citizenship Legislation Amendment (Strengthening Information Provisions) Bill 2020 and the Surveillance Legislation Amendment (Identify and Disrupt) Bill 2020 to improve human rights compatibility.

speeches.speaker: Michelle Rowland
speeches.brief: The Online Safety Bill was questioned for failing to address racist hate speech and incitement to violence targeting groups, citing the Online Hate Prevention Institute’s finding of a significant coverage gap and its call for an urgent takedown power covering incitement to hate. The question followed earlier queries prompted by the Christchurch terrorist atrocity and warnings on right-wing extremism.

speeches.speaker: Fiona Martin
speeches.brief: A question was directed to the Minister for Communications, Urban Infrastructure, Cities and the Arts asking for an update on how the Morrison government's Online Safety Bill will deliver on its plan to keep Australians safe online.

speeches.speaker: Paul Fletcher
speeches.brief: The speaker defended the Liberal-National government's record on online safety, noting the creation of the world's first children's e-safety commissioner in 2015, the handling of over 61,000 complaints, and $125 million in new funding. They announced a new Online Safety Bill to unmask anonymous abusers, increase criminal penalties to five years' imprisonment, and require removal of harmful images within 24 hours.

speeches.speaker: Tim Watts
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the government's Online Safety Bill is contradicted by its 41 refusals to force the member for Bowman to stand down as committee chair over his multiyear online harassment campaign, and by gagging 16 Labor women—including the members for Newcastle, Cowan, Jagajaga, Corangamite, Lalor, Cooper, Sydney, Franklin, Parramatta, Dunkley, Eden-Monaro, Macquarie, Griffith, Werriwa, Brand, and Canberra—who sought to hold him accountable.

speeches.speaker: Michelle Rowland
speeches.brief: Labor supported the Online Safety Bill 2021 as amended but criticised delays since the 2018 Briggs review, lack of process on online hate speech targeting groups, and the government withholding a report on age verification; the minister was asked for the third consecutive year what steps had been taken to address racist hate speech online.

speeches.speaker: Peta Murphy
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the government's failure to hold the member for Bowman accountable for his admitted online activities undermines the Online Safety Bill 2021 and the broader fight against domestic violence, where one woman is killed every week.
